## Reproducible Data Science

### The Importance of Reproducible Research: Main Steps

You should always show, how you got to the results of your research, so other people can check your research and reproduce it. They could potentially also
create new experiments based on your work, which means they need to be able to understand your reasoning and the steps you took to get to your results. 
The UZH has a center for [Reproducable Science](!https://www.crs.uzh.ch/en.html) that provides help and instructions on how to conduct reproducable science and research.

### Resources and Platforms 

- R
  R is a programming language widely used for statistical analysis and data science.

- RStudio
  RStudio provides a convenient environment for writing and running R code, managing files, and organising projects.

- R Markdown
  R Markdown allows researchers to combine code, results, and written explanations in one document.

- GitHub  
  GitHub helps track changes in code and makes collaboration in group projects easier.

- Tidyverse
  Tidyverse is a collection of R packages for data science.

- dplyr
  dplyr is useful for data manipulation, such as filtering, selecting, and summarising data.

- tidyr
  tidyr helps organise and reshape data into a tidy format.

- ggplot2
  ggplot2 is used for creating clear and informative data visualisations.

These tools help researchers organise workflow and make analyses easier to reproduce.


## The Art (and Science) of Plotting

### Plot Types

Provide an overview of the main plot types (including visual examples) and explain which types of data are best suited for each kind of plot.

### Colour Palettes

Explain how to use colour palettes effectively, which types of palettes are best suited to different kinds of data, and what factors should be considered when selecting an appropriate colour scheme.

It is important to choose appropriate colours to represent you data. The chosen palette should reflect the meaning of the variable. Colours make the figures more appealing and memorable. In papers/reports, you have to prioritize consistency and readability.

Types of palettes:
Sequential palettes: for ordered data or magnitude/intensity/frequency (Exp.: population density)
Diverging scales: data with meaningful midpoint or direction & magnitude of difference (Exp.: correlation from -1 to 1)
Categorical/qualitative palettes: for unordered/categorical data; no implied ordering (Exp.: countries)

It is important to consider accessibility when choosing colour palettes. For example, colour blind people won't perceive the colours the same way as someone who isn't colour blind. It is also important to check the contrast between light and dark backgrounds and text. Also, the number of categories matter too because too many colours may cause chaos and make the visualization unreadable. You also have to consider that the colour choices are safe if you want to print your visualizations. 

Useful ggplot packages for colours are: viridis, RColorBrewer and paletteer.

### *Ggplot2* cheat sheet

*ggplot()* initialises a plot object

Different type of plots:
    *geom_point()* creates a scatter plot
    *geom_line()* creates a line plot
    *geom_bar()* creates a bar plot
    *geom_col()* creates a column plot
    *geom_histogram()* creates a histogram
    *geom_boxplot()* creates a box plot
    *geom_violin()* creates a violin plot
    *geom_density()* creates a density plot
    *geom_smooth()* adds a smoothed line to the plot

Core aesthetics:
    *aes(x, y, color, fill, size, shape, alpha)*
    where x and y define the horizontal and vertical axes, color and fill control the color, size controls the size of points or line, shape controls the point symbol, and alpha controls the transparency.

Further parameters are 
    - *linetype* to control the line style (dashed, dotted or solid)
    - *group* to specify how observations are grouped

You can also adjust the labels and titles using *labs(title = "Your Title", x = "X-axis Label", y = "Y-axis Label")* and *theme()*, where labs() takes care of titles and axis labels, and theme(), like theme_minimal(), theme_bw() and theme_classic(), allows you to customize the overall appearance of the plot, including text size, font, background, and grid lines.
You can flip the axes using *coord_flip()*


## Compiling an R Markdown document

### Markdown Output Formats

The main output formats are HTML, PDF and Microsoft Word (docx).
#### HTML Markdown Format
HTML is usefull when publishing directly on a website, blogs and other online documentation because HTML is the standard language for websites.
#### PDF Markdown Format
PDF is usefull for a final report, papers, books and other finalised publications because it preserves its formatting over all devices.
#### DOCX Markdown Format
DOCX is usefull for collaborative work as well as files that need further editing.
